title: Shaheedi Jor Mela
hook: in December Sikhs gather at Fatehgarh Sahib to remember the younger Sahibzade

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maghi, and the Forty Liberated who came back. Your line was come back, anyway. Did you send that small message, or at least look at the door? Day one hundred fifty-four.

In the last week of December, while much of the world is between holidays, the roads around a town in Punjab called Fatehgarh Sahib fill with people. Huge crowds come. There's langar along the roadsides, kirtan in tents, a long, slow procession. But it isn't a celebration. Many families have spent the week sleeping on the floor instead of in their beds. Some give up sweets. The mood is quiet. They've come to remember two little boys and their grandmother.
screen: `A TOWN FULL OF PEOPLE IN DECEMBER.` → `NOT A CELEBRATION.` → `TWO BOYS AND THEIR GRANDMOTHER.`

segments.voice: The gathering is the Shaheedi Jor Mela. Shaheedi means of the martyrs. Jor mela is a gathering, a coming together. Here is what Sikhs remember. In December of 1704, Guru Gobind Singh's household left the fort at Anandpur after a long siege. At a flooded river, the Sarsa, in the dark and the chaos, the family was separated. The Guru's mother, Mata Gujri, went on with her two youngest grandsons: Zorawar Singh, about nine, and Fateh Singh, about six. A former servant, Gangu, took them in and then, tradition says, gave them up to the authorities. They were brought to Sirhind, to the Mughal governor, Wazir Khan. The boys were offered their lives if they would give up their faith. They refused. Tradition says they were ordered to be bricked into a wall, and they were put to death there. Mata Gujri died in the cold tower where they had been held. Two more details matter to Sikhs as much as the grief. The Nawab of Malerkotla, Sher Muhammad Khan, a Muslim, protested in open court that children must not be punished, and Sikhs have honored Malerkotla ever since. And a merchant named Todar Mal, tradition says, bought the ground for their cremation by covering it with gold coins. The town is now called Fatehgarh, after the younger boy. People sometimes say the boys were too young to understand what they were choosing. Sikhs remember it the other way: small, and yet they would not bend.
screen: `SHAHEEDI — OF THE MARTYRS.` · `SEPARATED AT THE SARSA RIVER.` · `TWO BOYS WHO WOULD NOT BEND.` · `MALERKOTLA SPOKE UP.` · then, large: `THE YOUNGER SAHIBZADE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is quiet. No doing. Sit still, and think of the two boys and their grandmother. You don't need to picture the wall. Picture them together, her hand resting on each small head. Then let the circle widen to children anywhere who are carrying things too heavy for them. If you pray, you can hold them all in Waheguru. If you don't, simply keep them company in the silence, the way you'd sit beside someone who is grieving. The bell holds the time.
Shaheedi Jor Mela. The gathering at Fatehgarh Sahib each December to remember the younger Sahibzade and Mata Gujri.

Your line: small, and unbending. Today, notice a child's courage: saying sorry first, trying again, telling the truth when it costs. And look back at this week: an unbroken reading, a Guru's birthday, cool water, lamps for the freed, strength in joy, and coming back. Day one hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: In late December, Sikhs gather at Fatehgarh Sahib for the Shaheedi Jor Mela with kirtan, prayers, langar and a procession; many families observe the week in mourning, sleeping on the floor and keeping celebrations away.

fork.setup: you're the Nawab of Malerkotla, sitting in the governor's court. two small boys are about to be sentenced. what do you do?
options: stay silent; it isn't your court.
protest that children must not be punished.
fork.reveal: he protested in open court. he couldn't save them, but Sikhs have honored Malerkotla ever since.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the martyrs' gathering. shaheed comes into Punjabi from Arabic, through Persian.

trapdoor: what it means: a gathering in mourning, remembering the younger Sahibzade and Mata Gujri at Sirhind.
what a scholar hears: the town was renamed Fatehgarh for Fateh Singh; the memory of Malerkotla's protest has shaped Sikh and Muslim relations in Punjab ever since.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 5, life of Guru Gobind Singh (Sirhind)

notes: Dates: evacuation of Anandpur and the Sirhind executions are given as December 1704 by many, 1705 by others. Confirm which to use.
Ages: commonly nine and six (some accounts eight and six, or nine and seven). Confirm.
Bricking into a wall is told as tradition; accounts differ on the manner of death. The script avoids graphic detail. Confirm.
Gangu's betrayal, Todar Mal's gold coins, Mata Gujri in the Thanda Burj, and Sher Muhammad Khan's protest: confirm details and names.
Mourning customs (sleeping on the floor, avoiding sweets or celebrations during the week) vary by family. Confirm phrasing.
